info.title: Employee MCP Servers
info.description:
Every Model Context Protocol server Cosmo Cargo crew members may point their AI assistants at, published from the same registry the gateway enforces at runtime. The 20 servers below are governed front doors to systems the company already runs on — Salesforce, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, SAP, Workday, Snowflake and the rest. None of them is a new system of record, which is what makes it safe to hand an assistant the keys.

## How the gateway works

Clients connect over streamable HTTP to `https://mcp.cosmocargo.space` and speak ordinary MCP. On every call the gateway exchanges the crew member's SSO session for a downstream token, so the request lands as *that employee* and the product's own sharing rules apply; refuses servers the caller holds no active grant for, advertising only the tools inside it; masks restricted documents, compensation fields and customer PII on the way back; and writes an audit record kept for seven years.

## Access and limits

New crew start with the Microsoft 365 and Collaboration servers. Everything else is requested per server through the crew access portal, approved by the requester's manager and time-boxed to 90 days — there is no permanent grant. Finance, HR & Procurement servers need a second approval from the data owner.

Each crew member gets 600 requests an hour across all servers, 120 per server, and 4 concurrent sessions. Tool responses cap at 1 MiB and sessions idle out after 30 minutes. Exceeding a limit returns `429` with `Retry-After` — back off rather than retry, because a retry loop against a metered warehouse is the most expensive mistake a client can make here.

## What is deliberately missing

Approving a payment, releasing a requisition, posting a journal entry, provisioning identity, resetting MFA, triggering a deployment, and sending mail on a crew member's behalf are all absent by design. Assistants prepare that work; a human commits it in the system of record, where the approval chain and audit trail already live.

servers.description: Sandbox gateway — synthetic data, no production records

tags.name: CRM & Customer Operations
tags.description:
Customer-facing systems of record: Salesforce Sales Cloud for freight revenue, Salesforce Service Cloud for enterprise support, Microsoft Dynamics 365 for the port services business, and Zendesk for consumer parcel support.

Every server in this group runs under the signed-in crew member's own identity, so a record an employee cannot open in the product is not reachable through the assistant either.

tags.name: Microsoft 365 & Productivity
tags.description:
Mail, calendar, chat, and documents through Microsoft Graph. These are the servers crews reach for dozens of times a day — finding the thread where a decision was made, booking a slot around a departure window, grounding an answer in the current standard operating procedure.

Mail is draft-only across the tenant: assistants may compose into Drafts but never send.

tags.name: Collaboration & Knowledge
tags.description:
Slack Enterprise Grid and Atlassian Confluence — the channels and wiki where operational knowledge actually accumulates. Incident reconstruction and runbook lookups dominate usage.

Private channels and direct messages are filtered out at the gateway for every crew member, regardless of scope.

tags.name: IT Service & Engineering
tags.description:
ServiceNow for incidents and the CMDB, Jira and Azure DevOps for delivery work, and Okta for identity context on service desk calls.

The pattern in this group is read broadly, write narrowly: an assistant can open an incident or move a ticket, but change approvals, pipeline runs, and identity provisioning stay with their existing controls.

tags.name: Finance, HR & Procurement
tags.description:
Workday, SAP S/4HANA, SAP Concur, Oracle NetSuite, and DocuSign. This is the most tightly governed group on the gateway: financial and worker data is masked or scoped to the caller, and the ERP servers are read-only.

Anything that posts a document, releases a requisition, or approves a payment is deliberately absent. Assistants prepare work here; humans commit it.

tags.name: Data & Analytics
tags.description:
Snowflake for ad-hoc SQL against governed reporting schemas, Power BI for questions against published semantic models.

Both servers carry hard cost ceilings — a dedicated extra-small warehouse with a statement timeout on the Snowflake side, row caps and read-only DAX on the Power BI side — so an agent stuck in a retry loop cannot spend the analytics budget.

post.description:
Pipeline, account, and activity data for the freight sales org. Every session is pinned to the crew member's own Salesforce user, so record visibility follows the sharing rules already configured in Sales Cloud — an account executive on the Outer Rim desk sees the Outer Rim book and nothing more.

Writes are scoped to opportunities, tasks, and activity logging. Quote approvals, contract terms, and anything that moves revenue recognition stay in Salesforce behind their existing approval processes.

post.description:
Case management for the shipment support desk. Support engineers use this server to triage inbound cases, pull the knowledge article that matches a customs rejection, and write resolution notes without leaving their assistant.

Case comments created through the gateway are stamped with an `MCP` origin so quality audits can separate assistant-drafted notes from hand-typed ones. Public-facing comments require the `salesforce.service:write` scope, which is granted per queue.

post.description:
Dataverse access for the ground-handling and port services business, which runs on Dynamics 365 rather than Sales Cloud. Field service work orders for dock crews live here, so this is the server that answers "which berth repairs are still open at Titan Port?"

The gateway calls Dataverse with the crew member's Entra ID token, so column-level security and business unit hierarchy are enforced upstream. FetchXML queries are capped at 5,000 rows and run against the read replica.

The consumer-facing parcel help desk runs on Zendesk while enterprise freight accounts are handled in Service Cloud. Agents use this server for backlog triage: find the tickets breaching SLA, summarise a long thread, and reassign to the right group.

Ticket macros and automations are intentionally not exposed — an assistant that can fire a macro can also fire a mass refund. Assignment is limited to groups the agent already belongs to.

Microsoft Graph access to the crew member's own mailbox and calendar. This is the highest-traffic server on the gateway: "what did the Kepler Freight thread land on", "find 45 minutes with the customs team before the Thursday departure".

Mail is draft-only by design. The server can compose a reply into the Drafts folder but cannot send it, so a human always presses send. Delegate and shared mailboxes are excluded unless the platform team grants an explicit delegation grant.

post.description:
The document tier: standard operating procedures, port handbooks, carrier contracts, and the manifest templates the operations team keeps in SharePoint libraries. Grounding an assistant here is what stops it inventing a cryo-handling procedure.

Retrieval is read-mostly. File contents are streamed through the gateway's DLP scanner, and documents labelled `Restricted — Legal` are refused with a 403 even when the user has NTFS-level access, because contract review has its own audited workflow.

Public channel history across the Cosmo Cargo grid, plus the ability to post as the signed-in user. Incident retrospectives lean on this server heavily: the assistant reconstructs the timeline from `#ops-anomalies` instead of a human copying timestamps.

Private channels and DMs are out of scope for every crew member — the gateway drops those conversation types before the model ever sees them. Posting is rate limited to 20 messages per hour per user to keep an over-eager agent from flooding a channel.

Delivery tracking for the platform, telemetry, and manifest engineering teams. The common path is sprint hygiene: what is unassigned, what is blocked, which issues haven't moved since the last departure review.

Transitions honour the project workflow, so an assistant cannot skip a required review state. Issue creation defaults to the caller's board and always sets the reporter to the signed-in user, which keeps the audit trail honest.

Repos, pipelines, and work items for the avionics and ground-control codebases that never moved to Jira. Release engineers use it to answer "which pipeline failed and what changed in that run" while they are still in the incident channel.

Pipelines are observable but not triggerable: no queueing runs, no approving stage gates, no editing variable groups. Deployment authority stays with the release approvers named in the pipeline definition.

post.description:
Read-only identity context for the IT service desk: who someone is, which groups they belong to, which applications they are assigned, and whether their last sign-in looks normal. It shortens the "I can't get into the manifest tool" call from ten minutes to one.

This server runs on a service token rather than user SSO, because it reads directory data on behalf of the desk rather than the caller. It is deliberately read-only — provisioning, group membership changes, password resets, and MFA resets all stay in the audited Okta admin console.

post.description:
Self-service HR: your own profile, your team, your leave balance, and the open requisitions you are hiring for. Crew rotations are long and time-off maths is fiddly, so "how much shore leave do I have left after the Vega run?" is the single most common question this server answers.

Scope is the caller and, for people leaders, their reporting chain. Compensation, performance ratings, and any other worker's private data are never returned, no matter how the question is phrased. Time-off requests still route through the normal Workday approval chain.

The financial and materials backbone: purchase orders for fuel and consumables, requisitions awaiting release, stock on hand at every port warehouse, and cost centre actuals for the fleet. Procurement analysts use it to reconcile a berth invoice against the order that generated it.

Carrier agreements, berth leases, and customs indemnity forms all move through DocuSign. The recurring question is status, not signing: which of the twelve envelopes sent before the Kepler tender are still waiting on a counter-signature.

Sending is restricted to templates that Legal has pre-approved, so an assistant can dispatch a standard NDA but cannot compose bespoke contract language into an envelope. Voiding requires the `docusign.envelopes:send` scope and is always logged with the crew member's identity.

The warehouse behind every operational metric: on-time arrival by corridor, cargo damage rates by container class, fuel burn per parsec. Analysts point an assistant at it to draft and refine SQL, then move the good query into a dashboard.
